claims.text: The initial MnNiSi-based alloy is bulk, polycrystalline, and relatively coarse-grained.
The initial alloy exhibits a high magnetic entropy change suitable for magnetic refrigeration.
The untreated coarse-grained material has suboptimal mechanical properties.
Cold rolling followed by optimized annealing will refine the grain structure.
Cold rolling followed by optimized annealing will homogenize the grain structure.
Appropriate annealing can refine the microstructure without triggering unwanted phase transformations.
Processing in an inert atmosphere will avoid oxidation.
The desired average grain size is submicrometer but not fully nanocrystalline.
Refinement into the nanocrystalline regime may disrupt magnetic exchange interactions.
The processing will produce a refined microstructure with a narrower grain-size distribution and well-defined grain boundaries.
Grain refinement will increase mechanical strength by Hall–Petch hindrance of dislocation motion.
Grain refinement will improve ductility through the Hall–Petch effect.
A submicrometer refined structure will preserve coherent magnetic-domain interactions required for a large magnetocaloric effect.
The proposed processing will minimize internal stress concentrations.
Internal stress concentrations can impair magnetocaloric performance.
Processed samples will have higher yield strength than the untreated coarse-grained baseline.
Processed samples will have greater tensile ductility than the untreated coarse-grained baseline.
Processed samples will show only a marginal or statistically insignificant decrease in magnetic entropy change under comparable field changes.
Secondary phases formed during annealing may disrupt magnetic exchange and reduce the magnetocaloric effect.
The rolling reduction, annealing temperature, and annealing duration needed for the optimal tradeoff are not yet determined.

contradictions.description: The hypothesis acknowledges that inadequate or overly aggressive processing may fail and that the optimal parameters are unknown, but the falsification rule says failure of any processed sample is sufficient to falsify the hypothesis. Nonoptimized members of the proposed processing series are therefore treated both as expected possible failures and as decisive falsifiers.
